g.title: Present simple and continuous; action and non-action verbs
g.rule:
Choose the tense by asking: is it always true / a habit, or is it happening now / temporary?

habits and facts → present simpleI usually cook at home. · She doesn't eat meat.
now or temporary → present continuousI'm cooking dinner now. · He's eating less sugar this month.
non-action verbs (like, know, want, need, prefer) → simple onlyI want a coffee. I'm wanting

Some verbs change meaning: I have two brothers (possess) but I'm having lunch (action).

ex.q: My sister ___ fish. She never eats it.
Be quiet, please. I ___ to the recipe.
This soup ___ delicious!
We ___ (not / usually / eat) out during the week.

talk: What do you usually eat on a normal weekday?
Are you trying to change anything about your diet at the moment?

g.title: Future forms: be going to, present continuous, will
g.rule:
English has no single future tense. Choose the form by the kind of future.

a plan or intention → be going toI'm going to visit my grandparents this summer.
a fixed arrangement (time, place) → present continuousWe're meeting my cousins at six.
a decision now, an offer, a promise, a prediction → willI'll help you. · I think he'll be a good father.

Use be going to for a prediction you can see: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.

ex.q: “The phone is ringing.” “OK, I ___ it.”
My brother ___ married in June. They booked the restaurant last week.
I've decided. I ___ more time with my family this year.
I promise I ___ (not / tell) Mum.

talk: What are you doing with your family or friends this weekend?

g.title: Present perfect and past simple
g.rule:
Both talk about the past. The question is: do we say when?

experience or news, no time given → present perfectI've bought a new phone. · Have you ever lent money to a friend?
a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020) → past simpleI bought it last week. It cost a lot.
just / already / yet → present perfectShe's already paid. · I haven't saved enough yet.

Conversations often start in the present perfect and continue in the past simple: “Have you ever wasted money?” “Yes, I bought a guitar and never played it.”

ex.q: I ___ my wallet yesterday.
___ you ever ___ anything online and regretted it?
We haven't paid the bill ___.
She ___ (already / spend) all her money.

talk: Have you ever bought something you never used? What happened?
Are you a spender or a saver? Give an example.

g.title: Present perfect + for / since; present perfect continuous
g.rule:
Use these forms for something that started in the past and is still true now.

for + a period · since + a starting pointI've lived here for three years / since 2022.
action verbs → present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)She's been working for a charity since May.
non-action verbs (know, be, have) → present perfect simpleWe've known each other for ages.

The continuous form is also used for a recent activity with a visible result: You look tired. Have you been running?

ex.q: How long ___ English?
I've had this job ___ last September.
They ___ each other since school.

talk: What have you been doing recently that is new for you?

g.title: Comparatives and superlatives
g.rule:
Compare two things with a comparative; pick one from a group with a superlative.

short adjectivesfast → faster → the fastest
long adjectivescomfortable → more comfortable → the most comfortable
the same / not the sameThe bus is as quick as the tram. · It isn't as cheap as the train.
adverbsShe drives more carefully than me.

Irregular: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further → the furthest.

ex.q: Cycling is ___ than driving in the city centre.
It's ___ journey I've ever made.
The metro isn't ___ the bus.
Trains are ___ (comfortable) than buses.

talk: What is the best way to travel around your city? Compare two ways.

g.title: Obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should
g.rule:
These verbs show how strong a rule or piece of advice is.

a rule or necessity → have to / mustYou have to switch off your phone. · You must be on time.
not necessary → don't have toYou don't have to bring a present.
prohibited → mustn'tYou mustn't speak loudly here.
advice or opinion → should / shouldn'tYou should say thank you.

Careful: don't have to (your choice) is very different from mustn't (don't do it!).

ex.q: It's a free concert. You ___ pay.
You ___ use your phone during the exam. It's forbidden.
I think you ___ apologise to her.
In my last job I ___ (have to) wear a suit.

g.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
g.rule:
Can has only two forms (can, could). Use be able to for all the others.

present · pastI can swim. · I could read when I was four.
futureI'll be able to drive next year.
present perfectI've never been able to dance.
after another verb or toI'd love to be able to speak Chinese.

For one successful moment in the past, say was able to or managed to: The test was hard, but I was able to finish it.

ex.q: I'd like to ___ play the piano.
She ___ speak three languages when she was ten.
I've never ___ cook well.
After this course you ___ (be able to) understand films in English.

talk: What is something you could not do before but can do now? How did you learn it?
What would you love to be able to do?

g.title: Past tenses: simple, continuous, perfect
g.rule:

the main events → past simpleThe match started at eight and we won.
background, an action in progress → past continuousIt was raining and the fans were singing.
something that happened earlier → past perfectWhen I arrived, the game had already started.

A short action often interrupts a longer one: I was running when I hurt my knee.

g.title: Past and present habits: used to, usually
g.rule:
Used to is only for the past. For a present habit, use usually + present simple.

a past habit or state that is finishedWe used to see each other every day. · I used to have long hair.
negative and questionI didn't use to like him. · Did you use to live here?
a present habitNow we usually meet at weekends.

Don't use used to for one single action: I met her in 2019 (not used to meet).

ex.q: We ___ be best friends, but we don't talk now.
I ___ call my friends at the weekend. It's my routine.
___ you use to play outside a lot as a child?

g.title: Modals of deduction: might, can't, must
g.rule:
Use these modals to say how sure you are about something.

g.title: First conditional and future time clauses
g.rule:
Talk about a possible future: the condition is in the present, the result uses will.

unless = if … notYou won't pass unless you work harder.
when, as soon as, until, before, after + presentI'll call you as soon as I get my results.

Never use will after if, when, unless, as soon as: if I will pass.

g.title: Reported speech: statements, questions and commands
g.rule:
When you report words later, the tense usually moves one step back.

statement“I'm busy.” → She said (that) she was busy.
will → would · can → could“I'll call.” → He said he would call.
question: no do / did, normal word order“Where do you live?” → He asked where I lived.
command: tell / ask + person + to“Wait here.” → She told me to wait.

Say something · tell somebody something: She said she was tired. She told me she was tired.

ex.q: “I can't find my receipt.” → She said she ___ find her receipt.
He asked me where ___.
The assistant ___ me to wait.
“We will refund your money.” → They said they ___ refund my money.
